edges.relationship: White credits Giddens with helping him understand cultural persistence and change as products of active transmission rather than opposites.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 written answer, read in Fontella’s Portuguese translation published 2022:13 and 16, explicitly gives Giddens greater weight than Wagner and describes the lens used to study Indigenous–European cultural change. At 16 he connects structuration with his criticism of upstreaming. The interviewer supplies the 1979/1981/1984 work dates; this answer does not independently identify which individual book supplied each insight. No fresh reading of Giddens’s originals, formal teaching or complete adherence is inferred.

edges.relationship: White acknowledges Lévi-Strauss’s earlier influence and adapts bricolage and cross-cultural coalition while qualifying his structuralist typologies.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 2011 preface: xiii/note 2, xvii–xix/notes 18–27 and xxiv expressly recalls substantial influence, admires his conceptual boldness, and develops particular resources from The Savage Mind and Race and History. White distinguishes these uses from rejection of rigid historical/ahistorical divisions; influence and criticism coexist. The editions cited in the preface and the 1952 pamphlet remain White’s references, not newly read originals; the 2011 retrospective is distinct from the 1991 book.

edges.relationship: White rejects rigid hot/cold social typologies and extends bricolage beyond a closed inventory of inherited cultural materials.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2011:xvii–xix distinguishes the more schematic structuralist readings from Lévi-Strauss’s own changing, nuanced statements. White’s hybrid societies can consciously create new rituals and structures; bricolage can incorporate new scientific elements. This is a specific disagreement with categorical and closed-system versions, alongside acknowledged debt and shared cross-cultural concerns, not a claim that Lévi-Strauss denied all historical change. Own translated 2021 answer at 2022:14 restates that qualification; underlying works remain unread.

edges.relationship: White uses Scott’s account of households, unstable alliances and refuges from state power to sharpen the comparative possibilities of the middle ground.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2011:xiv explicitly recalls admiring and using Scott, then credits The Art of Not Being Governed with developing a more theoretically powerful comparative account than his own earlier empiricism. Notes 6–9 identify Scott 2009:38, ix, 129–137 and 210–211. The specific interpretation is White’s substantive reading, not a fresh reading of Scott’s full book or evidence that the 2009 work caused White’s 1991 argument.

edges.relationship: In White’s account, Scott develops his earlier attention to households and provisional village alliances into a wider comparative analysis of state-resistant refuges.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2011:xiv reports Scott’s explicit credit at The Art of Not Being Governed 2009:38, then explains how Scott uses that insight differently and more effectively across Zomia and other regions. This is a relationship mediated through White’s named substantive discussion of Scott; the original Scott passage and full book are unread. It does not equate the pays d’en haut with Zomia or infer identical arguments or personal contact.

edges.relationship: Deloria questions whether the middle ground’s metaphor and dependence on balanced power limit its portability as an analytic concept.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 2006:15–22 distinguishes his admiration for White’s detailed research and cultural-production argument from concern about simplification, place/process slippage and a structural-equivalence requirement. At 21–22 he seeks more complex theories of power, and allows that new cultural production travels beyond the pays d’en haut; this is not a rejection of all comparison. White 2011:xii/note 1 explicitly credits Deloria’s sympathetic criticism with clarification. Existing White-to-Deloria writing-resource edge_2617 remains unchanged, with no second contribution arrow in that direction.

edges.relationship: White challenges Hofstadter’s account of Gilded Age individualism and weak government, emphasizing household ideals, cooperation and state intervention.
edges.evidence_note: Own Stanford interview, question on earlier historical interpretations and the following question on misconceptions, names Hofstadter jointly with Wiebe on laissez-faire, corruption and weak government, then singles out Hofstadter on individualism. White instead describes tariffs, subsidies and social provision, power delegated without sufficient administrative capacity, and the home as a political ideal. These are White’s attributed objections, not proof that every Hofstadter text neglects government or cooperation. Existing Wiebe critique edge_2340 retains its joint-target qualifications; complete monographs remain unread. Department repost dated 25 October 2017 is distinct from the linked original News Service item.

edges.relationship: Cook uses Harris’s account of provinces replacing local settlements and amorphous regions to support his challenge to regionalism as a historical unit of analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 1983 review:138 and 141, quoting and interpreting Harris’s chapter in Heartland and Hinterland. Cook praises its insight while saying it is not an adequate editorial conclusion; its provincial argument helps him draw a conclusion that may contradict the volume’s organizing assumptions. This is Cook’s substantive use of Harris, not a new reading of the original chapter or wholesale rejection of regional research. Existing field critique edge_944 remains unchanged.

edges.relationship: Cook invokes Berger’s history of English-Canadian historical writing to frame the displacement and reassessment of the national school.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 1983 review:137 characterizes The Writing of Canadian History (1976) as an epitaph that recognizes both accomplishments and failings and points toward new questions and synthesis. This is a bounded historiographical resource within Cook’s regionalism argument, not formal teaching or adoption of every judgment in Berger’s unread book. The national-tradition group critique retains its wider joint context.

edges.relationship: Cook credits McKay’s account of wartime Atlantic Canada with prompting reconsideration of the region’s place in the transformation of early twentieth-century Canada.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 1993 review:149–150 treats McKay’s synthesis of social, economic, cultural and political history, the Halifax Explosion and postwar labour conflict; Cook pairs this with Howell’s chapter when urging broader reconsideration. The resource is particular to these chapters and keeps Howell’s shared credit. McKay’s original chapter and later books are unread; praise does not prove agreement with every later McKay project.

edges.relationship: Wright reports that Cook credited Creighton’s encouragement and exacting standards during his doctoral research on J. W. Dafoe.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Donald Wright’s original 2016 remembrance, paragraph beginning “At Toronto”, identifies the supervision and quotes Cook’s 1963 acknowledgment. Their disagreements about French Canada and continuing friendship remain explicit; this supports a particular scholarly-training contribution, not adoption of Creighton’s nationalism. The original 1963 acknowledgment and thesis were not independently read. Wright’s 2017 chapter opening independently identifies the supervisor but mainly studies earlier formation.

edges.relationship: Wright reports Kealey’s acknowledgment of Cook’s early influence and their continuing intellectual exchange about the socialist journalist Phillips Thompson.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Donald Wright’s original 2016 remembrance, paragraphs beginning “He wrote a new introduction” and “Their many conversations”, distinguishes Kealey’s 1966 teaching encounter from later conversations and their joking Jimuel Briggs Society. This is a specific reported teaching and research exchange, not a claim that Cook supplied all of Kealey’s labour-history method or that later disagreements disappeared. Kealey’s original reminiscence and their correspondence remain unread.

Scott xiv/notes6–9; Deloria xii/note1; Lévi-Strauss xiii and xvii–xix; Dening xx–xxi; Havard xvi–xix and Merrell xix–xxiv checked. The 1991 book body and cited originals remain unread. pe135_cook_burden_1977.note: Complete own review 110–115 and its two notes freshly read in the original Acadiensis journal PDF. National versus regional focus, attribution to W. L. Morton, defined-region difficulties, shared benefits and shortcomings retained. Reviewed books, correspondence and underlying documents remain unread.

pe135_cook_unmasked_1983.note: Complete own review 137–142 and all eight notes freshly read in the original Acadiensis journal PDF. Berger’s historiographical framing at137 and the specific Cole Harris use138/141 support bounded personal-resource proposals. Graeme Wynn’s chapter receives the strongest chapter praise; his missing full endpoint is held. Cook’s qualified defense of class, sex, family and ethnicity research survives his rejection of regionalism as a general unit. Original chapters and cited books remain unread; the next review beginning on142 is a different signed text.

pe135_cook_atlantic_1993.note: Complete own review 146–152 freshly read in the original Acadiensis journal PDF. McKay149–150 is praised alongside Howell; Fingard and Reid receive similarly strong attention, and the closing argument keeps distinctiveness alongside shared historical processes. Book editors and chapter authors retain individual credit; no fresh whole-volume or chapter-original reading. Criticisms of contributors are Cook’s judgments, not independently certified factual errors.

rationale: Existing endpoints only; preserve named mediation, coauthorship, critical qualifications, edition and reading limits. All old graph records unchanged apart from append-only source reading notes. Tocqueville excluded as an owned dossier or newly read primary body, not as an existing resource endpoint in another historian’s own testimony. No new biographies, fields, life facts, chronology or dissertation analysis. OpenAlex remains paused.
